extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, PTO OED staff, and attorneys facing USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, conduct definitions, procedural requirements, and sanctioning criteria governing disciplinary proceedings against practitioners before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (initial decisions on default).

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of complaint (37 C.F.R. § 11.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: OED may serve a complaint on a respondent '[b]y mailing a copy of the complaint by "Express Mail," first-class mail, or any delivery service that provides ability to confirm delivery or attempted delivery to ... [a] respondent who is a registered practitioner at the address provided to OED pursuant to § 11.11,' or if the respondent is not registered, to the respondent's last address known to the OED Director. If a copy of the Complaint cannot be delivered ... the OED Director may serve the complaint 'by causing an appropriate notice to be published in the Official Gazette for two consecutive weeks, in which case, the time for filing an answer shall be thirty days from the second publication of the notice.' 37 C.F.R. § 11.35(a)(2), (b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service by certified/express/confirmable delivery to the address on file is required when respondent is registered; if undeliverable, service by two-week publication in the Official Gazette is authorized and starts the 30-day answer period from the second publication. The decision applied these rules where mailings to known addresses were returned as undeliverable and OED published notices in the Official Gazette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify OED of contact information (37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered attorney or agent must notify the 'OED Director of his or her postal address for his or her office, ... e-mail addresses ..., and business telephone number, as well as every change to any of said addresses or telephone numbers within thirty days of the date of the change.' 37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to keep contact information current can impede service and supports entry of default when OED cannot serve the respondent at addresses on file. In this case, returned mailings and undeliverable correspondence were central to service and default findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of failure to file an answer / default (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Procedural Rules provide that '[f]ailure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.' 37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If respondent does not file a timely written answer (including after service by publication), the allegations may be deemed admitted and the judge may enter default and decide sanctions on the admitted record. The judge may also decline to extend additional time for response to motions under 37 C.F.R. § 11.43 where respondent has not appeared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's authority on response periods (37 C.F.R. § 11.43)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Procedural Rules provide that the judge determines the time period in which a response to a motion must be filed. 37 C.F.R. § 11.43.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where respondent has not appeared or answered, the judge may limit additional extension of time for responses to motions; the ALJ applied this to deny further time and proceed to default resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner subjectivity to PTO Disciplinary Rules (37 C.F.R. part 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent is subject to the PTO Disciplinary Rules set forth in 37 C.F.R. part 10. See 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D); 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.1(h) and 10.20(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These Rules define the standards of professional conduct (duties to clients, public, and profession) applied in deciding whether misconduct occurred and in determining appropriate sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misappropriation / failure to remit client funds (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Misappropriating, or failing to properly or timely remit, funds received from a client to pay a fee required to be paid to the PTO, in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) and (b) via 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retaining client funds paid for PTO fees without forwarding them to the PTO supports findings of misappropriation and related disciplinary violations (also cited as basis for Counts 1–3 in the Complaint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting/receiving/retaining client funds but not incurring expenses (disreputable/gross misconduct) (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in disreputable or gross misconduct by requesting, receiving and retaining client funds for fees and expenses but not forwarding the client funds for fees or incurring expenses, in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conduct was treated as disreputable/gross misconduct that undermines fitness to practice; the Rules' list of examples is not exclusive, so analogous conduct may also violate §10.23(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation, e.g., by requesting, receiving and retaining client funds for fees and expenses but not forwarding the client funds for fees or incurring expenses, or by submitting a check to PTO that was drawn on insufficient funds and was dishonored, in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dishonest acts (including issuing dishonored checks related to client matters or PTO payments) constitute serious violations and may warrant exclusion; repeated or knowing misconduct aggravates sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to notify client of significant PTO correspondence (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to inform a client of correspondence received from the PTO when the correspondence (i) could have a significant effect on a matter pending before the PTO, (ii) is received by the practitioner on behalf of a client, and (iii) is correspondence of which a reasonable practitioner would believe under the circumstances the client should be notified, in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8) (implicating §10.23(a)/(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not notifying clients of Notices of Allowance, Office Actions, or Notices of Abandonment that could significantly affect a pending matter supports violations for failing duties to clients and can lead to abandonment findings and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect of legal matters entrusted to practitioner (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner, in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to respond to Office actions or to take steps to prosecute applications (resulting in abandonment) constitutes neglect and supports disciplinary sanctions including exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionally prejudicing or damaging a client (37 C.F.R. § 10.84)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally prejudicing or damaging a client during the course of a professional relationship, in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.84.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misappropriation combined with allowing abandonment and failure to act can be found to intentionally prejudice or damage a client and is an aggravating ground for severe discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conduct adversely reflecting on fitness to practice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the PTO, in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify under §10.23(b)(6) the conduct must not be prohibited by §10.23(b)(1)–(5); conduct duplicated by other enumerated subsections cannot also be charged as 'other conduct.' Case law guides the scope of 'other conduct.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of criminal statutes and convictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conviction of a criminal offense involving moral turpitude, dishonesty or breach of trust is expressly included in the list of conduct that may violate 10.23(c) (e.g., §10.23(c)(1)); state criminal statutes (e.g., Va. Code § 18.2‑181) may be evidence of intent to defraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuance of checks with insufficient funds can, under state law, create a prima facie inference of intent to defraud if not cured within statutory period; whether state criminal conduct constitutes a PTO disciplinary violation depends on (a) whether it fits §10.23(c) examples or (b) otherwise constitutes disreputable/gross misconduct under §10.23(a). The ALJ noted OED's reliance on state law but did not need to decide whether the conduct independently violated §10.23(a) given other findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the appropriate sanction the undersigned must consider, if applicable: (1) Whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to a client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession; (2) Whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) The amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; and (4) The existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors. 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four factors guide selection of sanctions (suspension, exclusion, reprimand). Aggravating factors include experience, pattern of abandoning clients, misappropriation, repeating misconduct after prior discipline, and failure to participate in proceedings; mitigating factors may reduce sanctions but none were found here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of discipline and duties of practitioners (professional duty rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of lawyer discipline proceedings is to protect the public and the administration of justice from lawyers who have not discharged, will not discharge, or are unlikely properly to discharge their professional duties to clients, the public, the legal system, and the legal profession. Attorneys who practice before the PTO have a duty to represent their clients competently and zealously, and to maintain 'the integrity and competence of the legal profession.' 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.21, 10.76, 10.83; ABA Standards cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of fitness to practice focuses on public protection and whether respondent can be trusted to fulfill professional duties; patterns of neglect, dishonesty, or misappropriation indicate unfitness and support exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and limits on restitution and remedial relief (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.20(b), 11.54, 11.56(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial decision may include 'an order of default judgment, of suspension or exclusion from practice, of reprimand, or an order dismissing the complaint,' per 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(a)(2). Procedural Rule 11.20(b) provides that '[w]hen the USPTO Director imposes discipline, the practitioner may be required to make restitution ... as a condition of probation or reinstatement.' The authority to impose restitution appears to rest with the PTO Director (final decision), not the hearing officer (initial decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OED may request restitution, but the ALJ concluded the initial decision lacks authority to order restitution as relief; restitution is more properly imposed by the Director as a condition of probation/reinstatement under 11.20(b) and 11.56(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible initial decision outcomes (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial decision will include '[a]n order of default judgment, of suspension or exclusion from practice, of reprimand, or an order dismissing the complaint.' 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where respondent defaults and allegations are admitted, the judge may enter exclusion (as here), suspension, reprimand, or dismissal depending on findings and sanctioning factors; the ALJ ordered exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal requirements and timing (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.54(a)(2), 11.55)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(a)(2), unless an appeal is filed with the U.S. PTO Director, the Initial Decision shall become the decision of the U.S. PTO Director thirty days from the date of the Initial Decision. Any appeal of this Initial Decision must be filed with the U.S. PTO Director within thirty (30) days after the date it is issued, in accordance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.55. An appeal must include a brief and exceptions to the Initial Decision and reasons in support; any exception not raised will be deemed waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely filing of an appeal with required brief and exceptions is necessary to preserve rights to administrative review; failure to timely appeal is treated as acceptance and waiver of further review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties and restrictions applicable to excluded practitioners (37 C.F.R. § 11.58) and reinstatement procedures (37 C.F.R. § 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent's attention is directed to 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 regarding the duties of excluded practitioners, and 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 concerning any future petition for reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion carries ongoing regulatory duties and prescribed processes for seeking reinstatement; these rules govern what excluded practitioners may or may not do and how they may petition for return to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of disciplinary findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The facts and circumstances of this proceeding shall be fully published in the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office's official publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication in the Official Gazette or other PTO channels is a customary part of discipline to inform the profession and public and to protect the public by publicizing sanctions.
